message.content:
### The “core” of most pop songs

In the vast majority of contemporary pop music the harmonic palette is **very diatonic**—you’ll find only a handful of chords that recur across thousands of hits.  The most common ones are:

| Function | Roman‑numeral | Typical quality | Example in C major |
|----------|---------------|-----------------|--------------------|
| Tonic    | I             | Major           | C‑E‑G              |
| Subdominant | IV         | Major           | F‑A‑C              |
| Dominant | V             | Major           | G‑B‑D              |
| Relative minor | vi     | Minor           | A‑C‑E              |
| Super‑tonic | ii          | Minor           | D‑F‑A              |
| Mediant | iii            | Minor           | E‑G‑B              |
| Leading‑tone | vii°      | Diminished      | B‑D‑F              |

> **Why these?**  
> • I, IV, V are the *primary triads* of a key and give the strongest sense of resolution.  
> • vi is the relative minor of the key and adds emotional depth without leaving the key.  
> • ii and iii are “step‑wise” chords that often serve as passing or pre‑dominant voices.  
> • vii° is rarely used on its own but appears as a leading‑tone chord in cadences.

---

### Most common progressions

| Progression | Roman numerals | Why it works | Pop‑song examples |
|-------------|----------------|--------------|-------------------|
| I – V – vi – IV | I – V – vi – IV | “Four‑chord” loop; each chord leads naturally to the next | *“Let It Be”* (The Beatles), *“Someone Like You”* (Adele) |
| I – vi – IV – V | I – vi – IV – V | Classic “50s progression”; gives a nostalgic feel | *“Stand By Me”* (Ben E. King), *“All of Me”* (John Legend) |
| I – IV – V | I – IV – V | The most basic “do‑re‑mi” sequence; very singable | *“Happy Birthday”*, *“Twist and Shout”* (The Beatles) |
| I – V – IV – V | I – V – IV – V | Adds a little tension by moving from V back to IV | *“I Want It That Way”* (Backstreet Boys) |
| I – ii – V – I | I – ii – V – I | Jazz‑influenced turnaround; gives a smooth cadence | *“Fly Me to the Moon”* (Frank Sinatra) |

> **Tip:** Even when a song uses a more exotic progression, the “core” of it will usually reduce to one of these patterns.

---

### How to spot them

1. **Listen for the “home” chord** – the one that feels like “the end.”  
2. **Count the beats** – most pop songs use 4‑beat measures; the chord changes often happen on the downbeat.  
3. **Identify the key** – once you know the key, you can map the chords onto the scale degrees.  
4. **Look for the “I‑V‑vi‑IV” loop** – it’s so common that many pop songs will have it at least once.

---

### Quick reference cheat‑sheet

| Key | I | ii | iii | IV | V | vi | vii° |
|-----|---|----|-----|----|---|----|------|
| C   | C | Dm | Em  | F  | G | Am | B°   |
| G   | G | Am | Bm  | C  | D | Em | F#°  |
| D   | D | Em | F#m | G  | A | Bm | C#°  |

*(Use the same pattern for any key; just shift the notes.)*

---

### Bottom line

- **Primary triads (I, IV, V)** + **relative minor (vi)** are the backbone of pop harmony.  
- **ii, iii, vii°** appear less often but are still part of the “toolbox.”  
- The most common progressions are simple, diatonic loops that resolve smoothly and are easy to sing along with.

If you’re writing or analyzing pop music, start by checking whether your chord sequence can be reduced to one of the patterns above.  Once you master those, you’ll have a solid foundation for exploring more adventurous harmonies.
